content: Midwifery traditionally refers to the practice of assisting women during childbirth. In modern healthcare, it encompasses the expertise of professionals who specialize in women's health, including prenatal care for expectant mothers, attending births, and providing postpartum care for both mother and infant. These professionals are called midwives, a term that applies to both women and men, and literally means with woman. Midwives are autonomous practitioners who specialize in normal pregnancy, childbirth, and postpartum care. They aim to support women in achieving healthy pregnancies and natural birth experiences. Additionally, midwives often serve as primary caregivers for general women's health and are trained to identify and manage deviations from normal health conditions. Obstetricians, on the other hand, are specialists in managing illnesses related to childbearing and performing surgeries. While midwifery and obstetrics can complement each other, they often differ in approach. Obstetricians are trained to actively manage labor, whereas midwives are trained to intervene only when necessary. Midwives refer patients to obstetricians when care exceeds their expertise. In many regions, midwives and obstetricians collaborate to provide comprehensive care, but in some areas, midwives are the sole providers available for childbearing women. Midwives are also trained to handle certain abnormal situations, such as breech births or posterior fetal positions, using non-invasive techniques. In some parts of the world, traditional midwives, also known as traditional birth attendants by the World Health Organization (WHO), are the only available providers for childbirth. Historically, midwives also treated conditions like female hysteria. According to the WHO, a midwife is someone who has completed a recognized midwifery education program, acquired the necessary qualifications, and is legally licensed to practice. Midwifery education can take the form of apprenticeships, formal university programs, or a combination of both. Midwives are responsible professionals who work in partnership with women, providing support, care, and advice during pregnancy, labor, and the postpartum period. They conduct births independently and care for newborns, including preventive measures, promoting normal birth, detecting complications, and implementing emergency measures when needed. Midwives also play a crucial role in health counseling and education, not only for women but also for families and communities. This includes antenatal education, preparation for parenthood, and extending care to women's sexual and reproductive health and childcare. Midwives can practice in various settings, including homes, communities, hospitals, clinics, or health units. The International Confederation of Midwives adopted a definition in 2005 that emphasizes the midwife's role in providing comprehensive care. However, this definition has been controversial, as it excludes traditional midwives who are often the only available providers in developing countries. Historically, midwifery has been one of the few medical practices dominated by women. From ancient Greece to the 18th century in Europe, the care of mothers and infants was considered a domain for women. In the 18th century, a division arose between surgeons and midwives, as male medical professionals began asserting that their scientific methods were superior to the folk practices of midwives. This shift is exemplified by figures like Justine Siegemund, a renowned 17th-century German midwife who authored the first female-written German medical text. During the witch hunts in Europe, midwives were often targeted due to their specialized knowledge of birth, contraception, and abortion. Some historians, like Gunnar Heinsohn and Otto Steiger, theorize that these persecutions were driven by demographic goals to repopulate Europe after the Black Death. This theory is supported by the subsequent rise in birth rates and the European population explosion. In the United States, modern midwifery is divided into two main categories: nurse-midwives and direct-entry midwives. Nurse-midwives were introduced in 1925 by Mary Breckinridge through the Frontier Nursing Service (FNS) to serve families in remote areas of Kentucky. This model, combining nursing and midwifery, proved highly successful, significantly reducing maternal and infant mortality rates. Nurse-midwives are advanced practice nurses specializing in obstetrical and gynecological care for healthy women. They often hold master's degrees and practice in hospitals, clinics, and private offices, delivering babies in hospitals, birth centers, or homes. They can prescribe medications in all 50 states and provide care from puberty through menopause. Nurse-midwives frequently collaborate with obstetricians for high-risk pregnancies. Currently, 2% of nurse-midwives in the U.S. are men. Direct-entry midwives, in contrast, are trained in midwifery without requiring nursing education. They learn through self-study, apprenticeships, or midwifery schools and primarily provide care in out-of-hospital settings. Certified Professional Midwives (CPMs) are direct-entry midwives who meet the standards set by the North American Registry of Midwives (NARM). CPMs are the only U.S. credential requiring experience in out-of-hospital settings. Licensed midwives are state-licensed practitioners, while lay midwives are uncertified or unlicensed individuals trained through informal routes. The American College of Nurse-Midwives (ACNM) accredits both nurse-midwifery and non-nurse midwifery programs. In the United Kingdom, midwives are independent practitioners responsible for antenatal, intrapartum, and postnatal care up to 28 days after birth. Most midwives qualify through direct-entry university courses, while nurses can become midwives through an 18-month post-registration course. Midwifery students receive financial support during training, and all practicing midwives must be registered with the Nursing and Midwifery Council. Many midwives work within the National Health Service (NHS), providing hospital and community care, while others work independently. Midwives advocate for natural childbirth and oppose the medicalization of childbirth, ensuring women retain choice and control over their birthing experiences. In Canada, midwifery was reestablished as a profession in the 1960s and is now regulated in several provinces. Midwives provide continuity of care, informed choice, and the option of home or hospital births. They consult with other healthcare professionals when complications arise. Midwifery education in Canada includes a four-year university degree, and midwives are integrated into the healthcare system with hospital privileges and the ability to prescribe medications. Legislation has made midwifery services accessible to a diverse population. In New Zealand, midwifery regained its status as an autonomous profession in 1990. Nearly all midwives are now direct-entry practitioners with a Bachelor of Midwifery degree. Women choose between midwives, general practitioners, or obstetricians for maternity care, with midwives being the most popular choice. Midwives provide care from early pregnancy to six weeks postpartum, focusing on normal pregnancy and birth. They consult or transfer care when complications arise. Midwifery care is fully funded by the government, and births can occur at home, in birthing units, or hospitals.
